passage:
Fifteen minutes before Diwali guests were due, the flat was full of flour and noise. Ayesha caught sight of Lakshmi, nine, quickly pushing a notebook under the sofa cushion.
"Did you finish your maths homework?" Ayesha asked lightly, still stirring.
"Yes, Amma," Lakshmi said, too fast, not looking up.
Ayesha put the spoon down. She noticed the tight shoulders and the cushion. She sat down beside Lakshmi, voice low. "Lakshmi, I'm not angry. If it isn't done, tell me and we'll work out a plan after the guests. I would rather know."
Lakshmi's eyes filled. She slid the notebook out. "Two pages left. I was scared."

qa.q: How many pages of homework were left?
qa.a: Two pages were left.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when noticing the cushion and the tight shoulders?
qa.a: Ayesha felt concerned and understanding, seeing that Lakshmi was frightened rather than careless. That is why Ayesha chose a gentle voice instead of scolding.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that made it safer to tell the truth?
qa.a: Ayesha put the spoon down, sat beside Lakshmi, kept her voice low and said she was not angry and would rather know. That made the truth easier to say.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when saying "Yes, Amma" too fast?
qa.a: Lakshmi was scared of being scolded. Saying it too fast and pushing the notebook under a cushion show the fear.

grounding: A mother notices a child lying about homework out of fear of punishment, and offers a calm, safe way to admit the truth.

passage:
The cracked blue vase lay in two pieces behind the curtain. Ira, Deepika's mother, found it while watering the plants. When Deepika, seven, came in from the balcony, Ira held one piece up but said nothing.
"I didn't break it," Deepika said at once. "The cat did."
"The cat did?" Ira asked, calm. "The cat can't reach the shelf, can she?"
Deepika's chin wobbled. Ira knelt down. "Accidents happen. I care more about you telling me than about the vase. What happened?"
Deepika whispered, "I was dancing and my elbow hit it. I thought you'd shout."
Ira hugged her. "Thank you for telling me. We'll glue it together."

qa.q: Where did Ira find the cracked vase?
qa.a: Ira found the cracked blue vase behind the curtain.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when finding the broken vase and staying calm?
qa.a: Ira may have felt disappointed or annoyed at first but chose to protect the truth-telling. Holding up the piece silently gave Deepika a chance to speak first.

qa.q: What did Ira say that made telling the truth safe?
qa.a: Ira said accidents happen and that telling mattered more than the vase. That lowered the cost of honesty and Deepika admitted the elbow.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when saying "The cat did"?
qa.a: Deepika was afraid of being shouted at. The wobbling chin and the whisper "I thought you'd shout" show the lie came from fear.

grounding: A mother notices a child lying about a broken vase, and a calm, safe way to admit the truth reduces the fear behind the lie.

passage:
"Harsha, what happened to the blue vase?"
"The cat did it."
"The cat? The cat was outside all morning."
"Maybe... the wind?"
Ayesha looked at Harsha's face. His ears were red and he was staring at the floor, twisting his shirt. She knew that look. It wasn't cheekiness. It was fear.
She sat on the sofa and patted the cushion. "Harsha, come sit. I'm not going to shout. I just want to know what happened. Vases can be fixed or replaced. Lies make me sad."
"...I was playing catch indoors."
"Thank you for telling me."
"Are you angry?"
"A little sad about the vase. Very glad you told me. Let's pick up the pieces together, carefully."

qa.q: What did Harsha first say broke the vase?
qa.a: Harsha said, "The cat did it."

qa.q: What was Ayesha thinking when she saw Harsha's red ears?
qa.a: Ayesha sensed Harsha was scared rather than cheeky, and felt calm enough to make it safe for him to tell the truth.

qa.q: Which choice helped Harsha tell the truth?
qa.a: Ayesha sat down, promised not to shout and said the vase mattered less than honesty, which lowered his fear.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling while he blamed the cat?
qa.a: Harsha was frightened of being punished, which is why he stared at the floor and twisted his shirt.

grounding: A parent notices a child lying about a broken vase out of fear, and a calm, safe way to admit it helps him tell the truth.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
I'm Vandana, and I'll never forget the week Kavitha, my ten-year-old, told me every night that her maths homework was done. "Done, Amma." Then the teacher's note came: five pages missing.
My first reaction was anger. I wanted to shout, "You lied to me!" But I looked at her face when I showed her the note. She went white and started crying before I'd said a word. She wasn't sneaky. She was terrified.
So I sat on the floor beside her. "Kavi, I'm not going to punish you for telling me the truth now. What's going on?"
She whispered that she didn't understand fractions and was scared I'd be disappointed.
We did the pages together that week. And we made a rule: if you're stuck, telling me is never trouble.
She tells me now, most of the time.

qa.q: How many pages of homework were missing?
qa.a: The teacher's note said five pages were missing.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when the teacher's note came?
qa.a: Vandana first felt angry and wanted to shout, then saw Kavitha's terror and felt her anger soften into concern.

qa.q: What change reduced Kavitha's lying?
qa.a: Vandana promised no punishment for telling the truth and set a rule that being stuck is never trouble, making honesty safe.

qa.q: Why had Kavitha been hiding the missing homework?
qa.a: Kavitha was scared of disappointing Amma because she didn't understand fractions, so hiding felt safer.

grounding: A parent notices a child lying about homework out of fear, and making it safe to admit the truth reduces the lying.

passage:
Caregiver's note, written by Alka, Eshaan's Nani, for his parents
Wednesday afternoon. Eshaan came home from school and said his reading log was signed. I saw his bag later: the page was blank, and there was a note from Ma'am asking why it hadn't been signed for a week.
When I asked him, he said, "Ma'am lost the page." He wouldn't look at me and his hands were shaking. I realised he was frightened, not naughty. Last month someone had shouted at him over a lost library book.
I made him a glass of milk and said, "Eshaan, you won't be in trouble for the truth. I'd much rather know."
He cried and said he forgot to read, and was scared to tell.
Next step: I signed today's page after he read to me, and I suggest we all tell him that forgetting is fine to admit.

qa.q: What did Eshaan say had happened to the page?
qa.a: He said, "Ma'am lost the page."

qa.q: What did Nani realise when Eshaan wouldn't look at her?
qa.a: Nani realised he was frightened, not naughty, and felt concern rather than anger.

qa.q: What would you advise Eshaan's parents, based on the note?
qa.a: Stay calm when he admits something and tell him forgetting is fine to admit, so he doesn't need to lie out of fear.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he finally told the truth?
qa.a: Eshaan felt scared and ashamed, crying as he admitted he forgot to read.

grounding: A grandparent notices a child lying about his reading log out of fear, and a calm, safe invitation brings the truth out.

passage:
Thursday night. Seema's diary.
Found Amma's blue vase in pieces behind the sofa cushion. Asked Joseph. "I don't know, Mummy. Maybe the cat?" We don't have a cat that comes inside. His ears went red and he wouldn't look up from his plate. I wanted to shout. Then I remembered hiding a broken cup under my bed at his age, heart thumping. So I sat on the floor with the pieces and said, "Whoever broke this won't be punished tonight. I just want to know, so nobody steps on glass." Long pause. Then a small voice: "It was me. The football." He cried. I hugged him and we swept up together. Next time I'll say the safe part first.

qa.q: What did Seema find behind the sofa cushion?
qa.a: Amma's blue vase in pieces.

qa.q: What did Seema feel on hearing "Maybe the cat?"
qa.a: Seema felt a flash of anger and wanted to shout, but also recognised Joseph's fear from her own childhood.

qa.q: What will Seema do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Say the safe part first, that nobody will be punished and she just wants to know, because fear of punishment was what made Joseph lie.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph once Seema said nobody would be punished tonight?
qa.a: Joseph felt safe enough to admit the football broke it, and his fear came out as tears and relief in the hug.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a child's lie about a broken vase, seeing the fear behind it, and offering a calm, safe way to tell the truth.
